newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION - SOUTH AFRICAN "N" SHARES - BY D.SYLVESTER.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - SOUTH AFRICAN "N" SHARES - BY D.SYLVESTER.

text.p: By David Sylvester, chairman Shareholders Association of South Africa

The debate on the issue of low voting "N" shares is gathering momentum. The supporters and detractors of the practice are airing their views on the practical, moral, political, and economic level as to whether this devise is appropriate in the new democratic South Africa desperate to attract foreign investment.
Section 196 of the Companies Act of 1973, as amended, sought to eliminate the practice of companies having any class of share with no voting right.
Any that existed at that time would be tolerated, but no company would be allowed to issue non voting shares in future.

The practice of non voting shares was not particularly prevalent at the time with Gentyre "B", Metals and Mineral "A", Rex Trueform "A", and Romatex "A" having no vote; while Anglovaal "A", Greatermans Stores "A", and Wooltru "A" only had a right to vote if certain dividend requirements were not fulfilled.
OK Bazaars and Reunert and Lenz warmed to the spirit of the Companies Act in 1975 by converting their limited rights "A" shares to ordinary shares.
For the next 20 years no new non or low voting shares appeared on the exchange as family dynasties turned to pyramid structures, known as holding companies, to entrench their control.
But in 1995 the JSE introduced new listing requirements which opened the door to limited voting right shares.

The reason for this change was never specifically stated, but it was widely accepted that it was to allow members of the black community, previously excluded from the mainstream of business, to acquire a controlling interest in substantial companies without having to make huge investments.
If this was the reason it has failed dismally. New Africa Investments (Nail) is the only "affirmative action" group to have utilised the mechanism.
The most impressive affirmative action coup, the change of control of Johnnic , was effected without resorting to "N" shares.
The culprits who flocked to utilise the devise are almost without exception the family and conglomerate controlled companies which already embraced pyramid control structures.
The extraordinary feature is that it could not have been effected without the acquiescence of apathetic shareholders - individual and institutional.

This is because the majority shareholders are typically prevented from voting in the resolutions proposing the creation of low voting shares. They therefore rely on mobilising the support of the other major shareholders, almost invariably institutions which invest the savings of the nation.

It is one thing for small minority shareholders to be apathetic, but quite another for the major mutual assurance companies, unit trust management companies, portfolio managers, and pension fund managers to practice indifference.

They are paid to maximise the performance of the investments administered and the beneficial owners of the investments have a right to expect that the fund manager has given the matter due consideration and either attended the meeting or completed a proxy form. The support they have recently shown for unbundling projects has resulted in handsome financial rewards.
A convincing argument can be made that acquiescence to the creation of low voting "N" shares is a dereliction of duty on the part of institutional investors.
At an annual general meeting it is one thing for shareholders to give the directors authority over the authorised but unissued share capital for one year.
It is quite another at a special general meeting to authorise the creation of a permanent low voting share structure which permanently reduces the rights of shareholders to such an alarming extent.
What are the factors for and against low voting shares? Spurious logic is frequently given to support the concept.

The main reason given by most of the prospectus outlining the creation of "N" shares are a combination of the following: the existence of two classes of investor - those seeking to participate in management and those just looking to capital growth and a passive role. This assertion is clearly without foundation as all ordinary shareholders initially provided the same amount of capital and should enjoy the same rights.
Another justification is improved tradeability. This, too, is a poor and untested assumption. In any event surely a sub division would be as effective?
Black empowerment - as outlined earlier has been used in only a few isolated examples to this end.

It is in the best interests of companies with good directors to ensure continuity and keep out predators. This argument is as spurious as it is frivolous; it is for market forces to regulate and judge management and their performance.

Finally the justification is advanced that shareholder approval is required before implementation and this sanctions the practice. If anything this pragmatic if unprincipled explanation reveals the moral bankruptcy of low voting share structures.
The reasons against the creation of low voting share structures are far more forceful.

It is clearly a violation of the spirit and intent of the Companies Act; it is frowned upon by most international exchanges; it is undemocratic and probably unconstitutional; it is plainly aimed at entrenching control and deliberately preventing hostile takeover bids which may well be in the best interest of minority shareholders; the rights of shareholders are dramatically eroded.
It is the right of a shareholder to be apathetic if they so desire; it should not be the right of controlling shareholders to isolate themselves from market forces.
The most frightening feature of the creation of the "N" share monster is that no thought has been given to how, and whether, the structure can be disassembled or collapsed.
When one cuts through the semantics the low voting share has only one reason for existence - to prevent a hostile takeover by entrenching control in perpetuity.

In the future things can go badly wrong, but shareholders will be powerless to tackle the poor performance as a result of the control structure. It is conceivable that the only way to protest will be to sell the shares and invest elsewhere. This is hardly a satisfactory arrangement for partowners of a business.

Supposing that an investor has paid a premium for ordinary shares in order to have a voting right, is it fair that at some time in the future "N" shares, which probably cost the investor less, get converted to ordinary shares on a one for one basis? As the "N" and ordinary shares rank equally in every other respect is it fair that they do not in terms of votes?
There is an interesting Catch 22!
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
